Deep learning approaches may facilitate the interpretation of complex, multidimensional biological signals, enabling predictive modeling of disease progression, therapeutic response, and patient-specific risk profiles. In this context, biosensors can be viewed not only as measurement tools but also as integral components of adaptive medical systems, in which sensing and decision-making are tightly coupled.

Beyond data analysis, computational approaches are expected to play an increasingly important role in biosensor design and optimization. Integration of multi-omics datasets may accelerate the identification of clinically relevant biomarkers and guide the engineering of sensing modules with improved specificity, sensitivity, and tunability. The historical reliance on trial-and-error screening is increasingly replaced by artificial intelligence assisted circuit design, where deep learning algorithms predict protein conformation, optimize promoter strength, and mitigate genetic cross talk before experimental execution. In parallel, advances in protein design, regulatory circuit engineering, and host chassis development will further expand the functional scope of biosensors, enabling detection of increasingly complex physiological states (Fig. 4).

Despite these advances, significant challenges remain in translating genetically encoded biosensors into clinical practice, including issues related to robustness in complex biological environments, long-term safety, regulatory approval, and standardization of device platforms. Addressing these challenges will require coordinated efforts across disciplines, spanning synthetic biology, materials science, data science, and clinical research. Ultimately, genetically encoded biosensors represent more than a class of analytical tools; they constitute a foundational technology for constructing integrated, intelligent, and adaptive biomedical systems. As these platforms continue to evolve, they are poised to enable a new generation of precision medicine strategies in which sensing, computation, and intervention are seamlessly interconnected.

figures.caption: Overview of genetically encoded biosensors for disease biomarker detection and clinical application. (A) Representative diseases and their corresponding biomarkers across various human systems. (B) Core architecture of a genetically encoded biosensor, consisting of sensing, regulating, and output modules. (C) Optimization of biosensor performance parameters such as sensitivity, dynamic range, threshold, and basal leakage, with the goal of tailoring the sensor response curve to meet precise clinical needs. (D) Translational applications from laboratory prototypes to clinical utility, including portable diagnostics, wearable devices, and living microbial platforms."

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Engineered biosensors for biomarker diagnosis and theranostic circuits. (A) CpxAR-based glucose diagnostic system. Glucose triggers CpxA kinase activity and subsequent CpxR phosphorylation ("P"), driving target gene transcription. Solid arrows denote protein expression; dashed arrows indicate CpxAR signal transduction and allostery. Hydrogel encapsulation enables glucose quantification in clinical samples. (B) Phenylalanine-responsive theranostic circuit. Phenylalanine-induced dimerization of a human PAH-derived module activates phenylalanine-degrading enzymes. Alginate-encapsulated cells effectively reduce toxic metabolites in human blood and mouse models. (C) A diagnostic system for bile acids with environmental adaptability. Utilizing the VFA0359 regulator and genetic logic gates, engineered bacteria specifically activate in the mammalian gut while remaining dormant in external environments. (D) A theranostic circuit utilizing the HucR repressor. Uric acid binding induces dissociation of the KRAB-HucR fusion protein, triggering signal output and uricase production, which maintains healthy serum uric acid levels and reduces renal crystal deposition in mouse models.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Comprehensive engineering strategies for optimizing the dose response landscape of genetically encoded biosensors as well as computational and machine learning approaches for sensor engineering, regulatory-element optimization, circuit design, and DBTL-guided iteration. The central diagram illustrates the interconnected performance parameters including sensitivity, dynamic range, response threshold, basal leakage, and stability. (A) Dynamic range amplification techniques involve increasing gene dosage, changing promoter and ribosome binding sites, or deploying multistage transcriptional cascades to maximize signal output. (B) Basal leakage reduction strategies minimize background noise by strengthening DNA binding affinities through directed mutations, optimizing core promoter sequences, or implementing posttranscriptional suppression via antisense RNA and degradation tags. (C) Response threshold modulation adjusts the operational sensing window by altering the ligand binding affinity of the regulatory module or by modifying the intracellular expression levels of the relevant transcription factors and two component systems. (D) Sensitivity enhancement focuses on steepening the response curve by increasing intracellular ligand concentrations through membrane transporter engineering, or by improving allosteric and phosphortransfer efficiencies. (E) System stability reinforcement ensures reliable long-term performance in complex environments through the chromosomal integration of genetic elements and the implementation of robust stabilizer circuits to buffer against external perturbations.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption: Future perspectives and paradigm shifts enabled by genetically encoded biosensors integrated with artificial intelligence. The central schematic illustrates the continuous sense process respond cycle where engineered biosensors detect disease biomarkers in real time to deploy precise localized interventions. On the left deep learning methodologies accelerate the identification of novel sensing modules and streamline systematic optimization processes including protein engineering and genetic circuit design. The bottom section highlights how this technological evolution drives a fundamental transition from traditional static reactive treatments toward dynamic proactive health management utilizing portable platforms. On the right accumulated long term monitoring data empowers comprehensive chronic disease management and accelerates new drug discovery. By continuously assessing treatment efficacy these data driven frameworks facilitate therapy optimization and adverse effect minimization ultimately realizing personalized and predictive medicine.
